# Reliability of Electronic Medical Record to Assess Patient’s Eligibility for Lung Cancer Screening: Analysis of Two Pilot Trials

**Authors:** Ryan Sabour; Mahnur Bharucha; Rhea Gandhi; Richard Echeverria; Victoria Nguyen; Wen-Pin Chen; Argyrios Ziogas; Sunmin Lee; Tan Q Nguyen; Hari B Keshava; Michael A Hoyt; Gelareh Sadigh

**Affiliations:** aDepartment of Radiological Sciences, University of California, Irvine, California. | bChao Family Comprehensive Cancer Center, University of California Irvine, Irvine, California. | cDepartment of Medicine, University of California Irvine, Irvine, California. | dDepartment of Medicine, University of California Irvine, Irvine, California; Coleader of Cancer Control Program for Chao Family Comprehensive Cancer Center. | eDepartment of Family Medicine, University of California Irvine, Irvine, California; Director of Family Medicine Medical Education. | fDivision of Thoracic Surgery, Department of Surgery, University of California Irvine, Irvine, California. | gDepartment of Population Health, University of California Irvine, Irvine, California; Chair of Population Health & Disease Prevention; Director of the Biobehavioral Shared Resource, UCI Chao Family Comprehensive Cancer Center & the UCI Institute for Interdisciplinary Salivary Bioscience Research. | hDepartment of Radiological Sciences, University of California, Irvine, California; Director of Health Services and Comparative Outcome Research; Vice Chair for Faculty Development; Associate Editor for JACR.

## Abstract

Accurate smoking history documentation in electronic medical records (EMRs) is essential for determining lung cancer screening (LCS) eligibility. We investigated the completeness of EMR smoking data, its concordance with patients’ self-reports, and its reliability for LCS eligibility after 2021 LCS United States Preventive Services Task Force guideline change.

Between October 2023 and November 2024, patients aged 50 to 80 years with a primary care visit in academic and community practices of a health system, who were current or former smokers or had an unknown smoking history based on EMR, and who were being screened for two clinical trials on interventions to improve LCS were enrolled. Participants completed an LCS eligibility verification survey, and EMR smoking data from the most recent visit before PCP encounter were extracted for comparison.

In total, 322 patients were included (mean age 62.4 ± 7.9; 58.1% male; 15.6% Asian, 1.2% Black, 61.4% White, and 21.8% other races; 45.7% Hispanic). Overall, 39.4% (127 of 322) had incomplete EMR smoking history to determine LCS eligibility. Among 167 smokers with both EMR and self-reported pack-year data, 85.6% (143 of 167) showed discordance in pack-year. Further, 26.2% (51 of 195) of patients with determined EMR eligibility (15.8% of 322 participants) had discordant eligibility based on self-report. Hispanic (versus non-Hispanic) patients were more likely to have incomplete EMR data to assess LCS eligibility (odds ratio, 1.68; 95% confidence interval 1.01–2.80) and discordant EMR eligibility with self-report (odds ratio, 2.34; 95% confidence interval 1.10–5.08).

This study highlights significant gaps in smoking history documentation within EMRs, with high rates of incomplete and discordant data, particularly among Hispanic populations.

Keywords: Discordance, electronic medical record, lung cancer screening, self-report, smoking history

## INTRODUCTION

Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer-related mortality globally, accounting for nearly two million deaths annually worldwide [1]. In 2011, the National Lung Screening Trial showed annual low-dose CT for lung cancer screening (LCS) in high-risk populations resulted in a 20% decrease in lung cancer mortality compared with chest radiograph [2]. Recognizing the importance of early-stage detection, the United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) established LCS recommendations in 2013 [3]. Since 2015, both CMS and commercial insurance plans cover LCS with no patient cost sharing. Utilization, however, remains low, with fewer than 16% of nationally eligible individuals undergoing LCS, as assessed by the 2024 “State of Cancer” Report by the American Lung Association [4].

One of the main provider-level barriers to LCS is failure of electronic medical records (EMRs) to notify physicians of patients’ eligibility for LCS [5,6], mainly due to incomplete smoking history documentation in the EMR [6]. Unlike screening for other types of cancer, in which eligibility is largely determined by age and gender, LCS uses a risk-based approach that primarily factors in age and smoking history, including pack-year and years since quitting [7], and therefore, any missing data in smoking history could result in inability to assess patients for LCS eligibility.

Few studies have reported on completeness of EMR in documentation of smoking status [8,9], smoking intensity (ie, packs per day or pack-year) [9,10], concordance of EMR documented smoking history with self-reported history, as well as EMR reliability in assessing patients’ eligibility for LCS [11]. However, all these studies were conducted before the 2021 USPSTF recommendation update that expanded age eligibility from 55 to 80 to 50 to 80, and decreased smoking pack-year eligibility from 30 to 20 and before the American Cancer Society 2023 LCS recommendations eliminating the quit date for former smokers.

Despite national efforts to improve LCS, in a 2023 survey of primary care providers (PCPs) and pulmonologists, inaccuracies of EMR to identify eligible patients was recognized as a barrier to LCS by more than half of providers [6]. Therefore, we aimed at providing an update on completeness of EMR in documentation of smoking status and intensity, its concordance with patients’ self-reported smoking history and its reliability to determine LCS eligibility. Our study offers updated insights following the 2021 guideline, with a unique emphasis on disparities affecting Hispanic patients who are underrepresented in prior LCS documentation studies. Further, we focus not only on completeness and concordance, but also on the clinical implications of EMR misclassification at the patient level.

## METHODS

### Study Design and Setting

This study is a secondary analysis of prospectively collected data from patients screened for two pilot clinical trials (Empower LCS and Empower Latinx) (clinicaltrials.gov: NCT06000683 and NCT06225414) [12,13] based on data from patients screened between October 2023 and November 2024 at a tertiary academic health center, affiliated community clinics, and Federally Qualified Health Center (FQHC). The two studies were approved by Institutional Review Boards 3439 and 4471, and an informed consent and a HIPAA authorization form were signed before data collection.

### Participants

Empower LCS [12] is a single-arm pilot clinical trial, and Empower Latinx [13] is a randomized pilot clinical trial. Both recruited patients eligible for LCS to test feasibility and efficacy of a multilevel intervention to improve LCS. Both trials required patients 50 to 80, who meet 2021 USPSTF LCS eligibility criteria by self-reported smoking history at enrollment and who had a scheduled PCP appointment (index PCP visit) within 3 months at one of our health system 11 affiliated academic, community, or FQHC clinics. The PCP requirement ensured that eligibility assessment was followed by a clinical encounter in which LCS discussions could take place, though prior PCP visits were not required. Empower Latinx trial protocol was later amended (effective 2025, not applicable here) to include patients having a PCP regardless of upcoming appointments. Empower LCS recruited English-, Spanish-, or Vietnamese-speaking patients of any race or ethnicity; Empower Latinx goal recruited English- or Spanish-speaking patients of Hispanic or Latino ethnicity.

Given the two pilot trials had similar enrollment processes and similar eligibility criteria (differing only by participant race or ethnicity) and used the same LCS eligibility verification questionnaire, we combined their data to increase sample size and diversity for the current analysis.

Eligibility criteria for the current study were patients aged 50 to 80 years with an upcoming PCP encounter (index encounter) at any of the 11 affiliated primary care academic, community, and FQHC clinics. All patients were smokers or former smokers or had an unknown smoking history based on EMR structured data and were being screened for participation in Empower LCS or Empower Latinx trials by completing an LCS eligibility verification questionnaire between October 2023 and November 2024.

Exclusion criteria included being a nonsmoker based on EMR structured data, a history of dementia, or inability to participate medically or cognitively, as evaluated by the EMR notes or study coordinator. Additionally, patients who did not complete a HIPAA authorization form were excluded from the study.

At the time of this study analysis in December 2024, Empower LCS was closed to accrual (n = 70), and Empower Latinx was still recruiting (n = 32 of 60 planned). For the present study, we included all Empower LCS participants (n = 70), all enrolled Empower Latinx participants (n = 32), and individuals who completed LCS eligibility verification and HIPAA authorization but were ineligible for the trials (n = 220), yielding a total analytic sample of 322.

### Recruitment

Patient outreach for the two trials was through e-mail invitations via Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap) [14,15] with three e-mail reminders in patients’ preferred language based on EMR. In addition to reminders, nonresponders received a one-time text message. Additionally, we used outreach via mail, telephone, and in person in the clinic by bilingual study coordinator as backup for those without valid e-mail address and a convenience sample (30%) of nonresponders as was feasible by study resources.

### Self-Reported Smoking History

Self-reported smoking history was collected via a structured 2-min LCS eligibility verification survey that was aimed at assessing eligibility for enrollment in Empower LCS and Latinx trials. This survey was administered electronically via institutional REDCap [14,15], on paper during primary care clinic visits, or via telephone in patients’ preferred language. The survey inquired about smoking status (current, former, or never smoker), average number of cigarettes smoked per day, total years of smoking, and years since quitting.

### EMR-Record Smoking History

EMR-recorded smoking history including smoking status, average number of cigarettes smoked per day, total years of smoking, average smoking pack-year, and years since quitting was extracted using EMR search function from the most recent encounter with available smoking data that was before patients’ index PCP encounter. If all components of smoking history could not be extracted from a single encounter note, notes from different encounters were used. Extracted data were based on both structured and free text data available in the note. Our EMR has structured fields corresponding to each of the smoking history components outlined previously. Documentation can be completed by medical assistants during patient rooming or by the providers (eg, physician or advanced practice provider), but some providers may instead use free text entries.

The rational for data extraction before index PCP visit was to assess reliability of using EMR data to determine patients’ LCS eligibility before PCP visit. PCP time constraints to verify LCS eligibility and lack of EMR notification are known provider-level barriers [6], and although EMR health maintenance flags are a solution to this barrier, they are often not triggered due to incomplete smoking history documentation. Smoking history data extraction before index PCP visit enables assessing the scope of problem.

### Sociodemographic Information

We further extracted patient sociodemographic information including age, gender at birth, self-reported race and ethnicity, primary language, marital status, employment status, health insurance, and full address and zip code from EMR or self-reported surveys for patients enrolled in Empower LCS and Latinx trials. Area Deprivation Index (ADI) national percentile scores were calculated based on patients’ full addresses mapped to census block groups using the University of Wisconsin Neighborhood Atlas [16,17]. The ADI involves neighborhood socio-economic indicators such as income, education, employment, housing, and health care access. The score ranges between 0 and 100, with higher scores indicating greater socio-economic disadvantage. Index PCP encounter practice type (academic, community, and FQHC) was extracted.

### Statistical Analysis

Descriptive statistics were used to report continuous variables as mean and SD, and categorical variables as frequency and percentage. LCS eligibility based on self-reported smoking history and EMR data were determined using the 2021 USPSTF guidelines [18]. Discordance rate between self-reported and EMR documented pack-year as well as LCS eligibility was assessed using McNemar’s test for categorical variables. Discordance in pack-year was calculated as absolute discordance. We further assessed discordance in LCS eligibility, defined as any difference in LCS eligibility classification between EMR and self-report, regardless of which one classified patient as LCS eligible.

Univariable and multivariable logistic regression analyses were performed to assess patient-level and practice-level factors associated with incomplete smoking history documentation (dependent variable) or discordance between EMR and self-reported smoking history (dependent variable). Covariates for the univariable model included age, gender at birth, race, ethnicity, primary language, marital status, employment status, insurance type, ADI, and practice type. Variables with P <.05 in univariable analyses, as well as those selected a priori based on clinical relevance and prior literature, were included in the multivariable models. Multicollinearity among variables was assessed. Given concern for multicollinearity between language and ethnicity, only ethnicity was included in the multivariable model. A complete case analysis was conducted. Statistical significance was set at P < .05. All analyses were performed using SAS v9.4 (SAS Institute Inc., Carey. NC).

## RESULTS

### Participant Characteristics

A total of 6,745 patients were contacted to participate in the two trials, and 1,309 responded (19.4% response rate to outreach). A total of 56.8% (744 of 1,309) of outreach responders were interested in participating in one of the two trials. A total of 322 patients were included in the current study (Fig. 1).

*Fig. 1.: Patient recruitment and inclusion flowchart. LCS = lung cancer screening.*

Baseline characteristics of participants are shown in Table 1. Participants’ mean age ± SD was 62.4 ± 7.9. A total of 58.1% (187 of 322) of participants were male. Participants’ racial background were Asian (15.6%; 50 of 321), Black (1.2%; 4 of 321), White (61.4%; 197 of 321) and other (21.8%; 70 of 321). Ethnically, Hispanic (45.7%; 147 of 322) patients represented a significant portion of the sample set. Based on self-report data, 24.5% (79 of 322) were current smokers, 66.8% (215 of 322) were former smokers, and 8.7% (28 of 322) had never smoked before.

### EMR Smoking History Documentation Completeness

Although smoking status was available in the EMR for 96.9% (312 of 322) of participants, 42.8% of smokers (127 of 297) missed data on their pack-year cigarette smoking, and 15% of former smokers (31 of 206) missed data on their quit year in the EMR (Table 2). Therefore, for 39.4% (127 of 322) of participants LCS eligibility could not be determined based on EMR data.

### Discordance Between Self-Reported and EMR Smoking History

Among 167 smokers with available pack-year history data both in EMR and based on self-report, 85.6% (143 of 167) had a discordance in pack-year. Figure 2 shows absolute discordance in pack-year between EMR and self-report.

*Fig. 2.: Pack-year (PY) discordance between electronic medical record (EMR) and self-report (SR), stratified based on EMR eligibility for lung cancer screening with 60 being eligible and 104 not eligible. White color represents concordance between EMR and self-reported pack-year. Patterned colors represent scenarios in which EMR pack-year was more than self-reported pack-year. Nonpatterned colors represent scenarios in which EMR pack-year was less than self-reported pack-year. Darker colors represent a higher degree of discordance. Absolute discordance numbers (EMR-SR) in pack-year are shown. Discordance rates relative to EMR pack-year (EMR-SR/EMR) is not shown.*

Among 195 patients (with any smoking status) for whom LCS eligibility could be determined based on EMR, 26.2% (51 of 195) (15.8% of all 322 participants) had discordant eligibility when compared with self-reported data (P = .001). Among 135 patients not LCS eligible based on EMR, 83 (61.5%) were eligible based on self-report. Overall agreement between two sources for LCS eligibility was κ = 0.45 (95% CI 0.32–0.52) (Table 4).

In multivariable analysis, Hispanics or Latinos were more likely to have discordance between EMR-documented and self-reported LCS eligibility criteria (adjusted odds ratio = 2.34, 95% CI 1.10–5.08) (Table 3).

## DISCUSSION

Secondary analysis of data from two prospective clinical trials conducted between 2023 and 2024 revealed our institutional EMR was insufficient for accurately determining LCS eligibility in 55.2% (178 of 322) of participants, with 39.4% (127 of 322) having incomplete documentation and 15.8% (51 of 322) showing discordance between EMR and self-reported eligibility. Our study confirms persistent challenges in smoking history documentation that undermine accurate LCS eligibility assessment.

Our study data collected 2 years after USPSTF recommendation update remain similar to the studies conducted before 2021 USPSTF recommendation. In contrast to earlier studies that evaluated EMR documentation before the 2021 USPSTF guideline changes, our study includes an oversampled Hispanic cohort to provide a more nuanced understanding of disparities in documentation. In a 2016–2017 study, Patel et al found 41% incomplete EMR documentation rate and a 23% EMR and self-report discordance in eligibility rate [10]. In another 2014–2016 study, there was 96% discordance between pack-year documented in EMR and self-report, slightly higher than 85.6% reported in the current study [11]. Of note, there was 85% underreporting of smoking intensity (ie, pack-year) in EMR [11], and our study observed both under- and overreporting of pack-year. In the current study, underreporting of pack-year in EMR compared with self-report was more common than overreporting (68% versus 22%) among individuals ineligible for LCS based on EMR, which may contribute to low LCS uptake, as patients with underreported pack-years may not be flagged as eligible by EMR health maintenance tool. Among patients classified as eligible by EMR, underreporting remained the predominant trend (43%), followed by overreporting (39%). Although the survey and EMR information are both patient reported, discordance in the data might be due barriers in patient communication, specifically in cases of patients with limited English proficiency or low health literacy, as well as the temporal effect with EMR information having been recorded earlier than the self-reported survey. We did not document the encounter date of smoking history extraction from EMR and cannot assess the temporal effect. However, if EMR smoking data from prior encounters are expected to be the source data for tools such as health maintenance to address PCP barriers during their encounters, the current status of smoking status in EMR is not reliable.

Our study showed Hispanic patients are more likely to have incomplete EMR data for LCS eligibility or discordance between EMR versus self-reported eligibility. Hispanic patients, particularly those with limited English proficiency, face added communication challenges when provider-patient language discordance exists. Prior study showed only 60% of physicians and 37% of nurses use interpretive services for patients with limited English proficiency [19]. Additionally, encounter with these patients may be shorter [19], potentially limiting EMR documentation and contributing to disparities in screening. Greater providers’ cultural competency and frequent use of interpretive services may help reduce this gap.

Frequent documentation and update of smoking history through previsit questionnaires in the patient portal could improve EMR completeness [20]. In our study population, which oversampled Hispanics, portal use was 48% compared with 61.3% nationally. Therefore, portal questionnaires may not reach all patients, particularly since Hispanic patients are less likely to be offered portal access [20], further contributing to disparities. Another limitation is that smoking history entered in portals often does not automatically populate structured EMR fields and requires manual provider verification, creating inefficiencies. Patients who use portals are also more likely to discuss LCS with their provider [21], but, if providers enter smoking data as free text, it fail to trigger automated alerts or clinical decision support tools. Encouraging providers to consistently use structured EMR fields may help.

A 2023 study showed unstructured clinician notes captured smoking history more accurately than structured entries [22], which were present for only 12.5% of patients. Natural language processing (NLP) applied to unstructured clinician notes identified smoking history in 41.8% of cases [22]. A hybrid approach using NLP to map free text into structured EMR fields, and flag inconsistencies for health care provider review, could reduce manual verification, improve data completeness, and enhance screening uptake [23]. However, implementing NLP across health care systems faces challenges including validation requirements, integration into EMR workflows, and clinician acceptance, and ongoing provider review may still be needed, limiting scalability.

Pay-for-performance programs have shown to improve smoking status documentation [24]. Such efforts can be expanded to include quantitative pack-year tracking, NLP-validated data integration, and increasing LCS rates. Further, implementation of smoking documentation reminders built into the EMR may also enhance completeness, as demonstrated for smoking cessation efforts [25]. Lastly, others have shown an EMR-derived multivariable prediction model can aid in identification of LCS-eligible patients, but this also requires availability of smoking history data in the EMR to feed the model [26].

Our cohort consisted of patients who were interested to participate in clinical trials, which may limit the representativeness of the sample relative to the broader clinic population. As a single-center study, generalizability may be limited by institutional documentation practices. Further, provider documentation practices may vary across departments, influencing completeness. Our outreach response rate was 19.4% despite multimodality outreach effort, which may also impact generalizability. However, due to focus of Empower Latinx trial on Hispanic population, we oversampled Hispanic patients compared with our catchment area. Both EMR and survey data are self-reported, and we acknowledge the absence of an objective reference standard. However, the structured and standardized nature of survey collection—administered by trained bilingual research staff at the point of enrollment using dedicated prompts—likely improved completeness and reduced underreporting compared with routine EMR documentation, which is often updated inconsistently. We did not systematically evaluate whether smoking history was updated after the index PCP encounter as PCPs for patients enrolled in Empower LCS and Latinx trials were actively receiving alerts on their patients LCS eligibility, and hence this may impact their documentation of smoking history within the context of the clinical trial. We also did not control for prior longitudinal PCP relationships. Future studies should evaluate whether enhanced EMR accuracy translates to reduced screening disparities, particularly among populations with historically low LCS adherence.

- This study highlights significant gaps in smoking history documentation within EMRs, with high rates of incomplete and discordant data.

- Hispanic patients are more likely to have incomplete EMR data to assess LCS eligibility.

- These discrepancies pose a direct barrier to LCS eligibility determination and demonstrate a need for systematic improvements in smoking history documentation.
